points.title: Formula for the size of a text
points.must: Size = number of characters × bits (bytes) per character; ÷8 → bytes, ÷1024 → KB; metadata/formatting ignored unless told.
points.model: Size (bits) = number of characters × bits per character. ÷ 8 → bytes, ÷ 1024 → KB, ÷ 1024 → MB. Formatting and metadata are ignored unless the question mentions them.

points.title: Bit, byte, kilobyte
points.must: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes (KiB; use 1000 only if told); 1 MB = 1024 KB.
points.model: Bit = one binary digit (0 or 1). Byte = 8 bits = one ASCII character. 1 KB = 1024 bytes (follow the question if it says 1000). 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB.

points.title: What counts as a character
points.must: Letters, every digit separately, every space, punctuation and symbols, new-line characters if mentioned (CR+LF = 2 on Windows); quotation marks around the question text are not counted; counting example ("NIS Astana, 2026!" = 17).
points.model: Count letters, each digit ("2026" = 4 characters), every space, all punctuation and symbols, and new lines if told (Windows CR+LF = 2, Linux LF = 1). Do not count the quotation marks the question puts round the text. "NIS Astana, 2026!" = 9 letters + 2 spaces + 4 digits + 2 punctuation = 17 characters.

points.title: Size of one character
points.must: ASCII 8 bits = 1 byte; 16-bit Unicode = 2 bytes; UTF-32 = 4 bytes; UTF-8 1–4 bytes; 7-bit ASCII if the question says so (work in bits).
points.model: ASCII / extended ASCII: 8 bits = 1 byte. 16-bit Unicode (UTF-16): 2 bytes. UTF-32: 4 bytes. UTF-8: 1, 2, 3 or 4 bytes depending on the character. If told 7 bits (or another code size), work in bits and ÷ 8 at the end.

points.title: Steps of the calculation
points.must: Count → identify bytes per character → multiply → convert → answer with unit, round at the end; worked example "Hello, World!" (13 chars → 13 bytes ASCII, 26 bytes Unicode, 104 bits).
points.model: 1) Count every character. 2) Bytes/bits per character from the question. 3) Multiply. 4) Convert units. 5) Answer with unit, round only at the end. "Hello, World!" = 13 characters → ASCII 13 bytes (104 bits), 16-bit Unicode 26 bytes, UTF-32 52 bytes.

points.title: Fixed-length fields example
points.must: Names in 30-character fields, 25 students, 16-bit Unicode: 30 × 2 = 60 bytes × 25 = 1500 bytes = 1.46 KB; field size used, not name length.
points.model: 25 names × 30-character fields × 2 bytes = 1500 bytes ÷ 1024 = 1.46 KB. In a fixed-length field the full field size is used even for short names (padded with spaces).

points.title: SMS limit
points.must: 140 bytes = 1120 bits; 7-bit code → 160 characters; 16-bit Unicode (Cyrillic/emoji) → 70 characters.
points.model: One SMS = 140 bytes = 1120 bits. Latin-only: 7-bit code → 1120 ÷ 7 = 160 characters. With Kazakh/Cyrillic letters or emoji: 16-bit Unicode → 1120 ÷ 16 = 70 characters.

points.title: Fixed- and variable-length encoding
points.must: Fixed: every character same size (ASCII 1, UTF-32 4) → characters × size; variable (UTF-8; UTF-16 for emoji) → group characters and add.
points.model: Fixed-length encoding: every character the same size (ASCII 1 byte, UTF-32 4 bytes) → size = characters × bytes per character. Variable-length (UTF-8, UTF-16 for emoji): different characters have different sizes → group the characters and add the bytes.

points.title: UTF-8 sizes by type of character and a mixed-text calculation
points.must: ASCII 1, Cyrillic/Kazakh 2, Chinese/€/₸ 3, emoji 4 bytes; "Сәлем, әлем!" 12 characters: UTF-8 9×2+3×1 = 21, UTF-16 24, UTF-32 48, ASCII impossible.
points.model: UTF-8: English letters, digits, space, punctuation 1 byte; Cyrillic incl. Kazakh 2 bytes; Chinese, €, ₸ 3 bytes; emoji 4 bytes. "Сәлем, әлем!" = 12 characters (9 Cyrillic + 3 ASCII): UTF-8 9 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 21 bytes; UTF-16 12 × 2 = 24 bytes; UTF-32 48 bytes; ASCII not possible.

points.title: Emoji in calculations
points.must: Emoji = 4 bytes in UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32; "OK 👍": UTF-8 7, UTF-16 10, UTF-32 16 bytes; follow the question if it says 2 bytes per character.
points.model: A simple emoji is 4 bytes in UTF-8, UTF-16 (surrogate pair) and UTF-32. "OK 👍" = 4 characters: UTF-8 3 + 4 = 7 bytes; UTF-16 6 + 4 = 10 bytes; UTF-32 16 bytes. If the question says 2 bytes per character, use 2.

points.title: Which encoding is smallest
points.must: English → UTF-8 (= ASCII, half of UTF-16); Cyrillic → UTF-8 ≈ UTF-16; Chinese → UTF-16 smaller (2 vs 3); UTF-32 always largest.
points.model: English text: UTF-8 smallest (same as ASCII, half of UTF-16). Cyrillic: UTF-8 and UTF-16 nearly equal (2 bytes per letter, spaces 1 byte in UTF-8). Chinese/Japanese: UTF-16 smaller (2 bytes vs 3). UTF-32 always the largest.

points.title: Large documents
points.must: Characters = pages × lines × characters per line, or words × average characters per word; worked example with KB/MB (300 pages × 40 × 60 = 720 000 chars × 2 = 1 440 000 bytes = 1406.25 KB = 1.37 MB).
points.model: Characters = pages × lines × characters per line (or words × average characters per word incl. space). Textbook: 300 × 40 × 60 = 720 000 characters × 2 bytes = 1 440 000 bytes ÷ 1024 = 1406.25 KB ÷ 1024 = 1.37 MB. Report: 2500 words × 6 = 15 000 × 2 = 30 000 bytes = 29.30 KB.

points.title: Working backwards
points.must: Characters = size in bytes ÷ bytes per character; bits per character = size in bits ÷ characters; examples (4 KB / 2 = 2048 chars; 2000 bytes for 1000 chars = 16 bits → Unicode; 24 bytes of 6-bit code = 32 chars).
points.model: Number of characters = size (bytes) ÷ bytes per character: 4 KB = 4096 bytes ÷ 2 = 2048 characters. Bits per character = size (bits) ÷ characters: 16 000 bits ÷ 1000 = 16 → 16-bit Unicode. 24 bytes = 192 bits ÷ 6-bit code = 32 characters.

points.title: Transmission time
points.must: Bit rate definition (bits per second); time = size in bits ÷ bit rate; convert bytes to bits first; example 1 440 000 bytes × 8 = 11 520 000 bits ÷ 2 000 000 = 5.76 s.
points.model: Bit rate = bits transmitted per second (bps, Mbps). Time (s) = size in bits ÷ bit rate. Convert bytes → bits (× 8) first. 1 440 000 bytes × 8 = 11 520 000 bits ÷ 2 Mbps (2 000 000 bps) = 5.76 s; in ASCII half the time.
